name: Gideon

seo.title: Gideon in the Bible: the fleece, the 300 and his story
seo.description: Gideon in plain words: the farmer called from a winepress, the fleece, the 300 with jars and torches, the crown he refused, and his feast days.

band.lede: The farmer God called out of hiding. With 300 men, jars and torches, he routed Midian. Then he refused a crown.

picture.alt: A colour Bible picture at night: Gideon, young and red-haired, in a helmet, a mail shirt and a red cloak, strides forward blowing a long trumpet and holding a blazing torch high over his head. His men follow on either side, blowing trumpets and lifting torches under a dark, starry sky. A broken jar lies on the path.

card.line: The farmer called from a winepress, who led 300 men against Midian and refused a crown.

who: Gideon was a farmer of the tribe of Manasseh, in the time of the Judges. An angel found him threshing wheat in hiding and sent him to save Israel from Midian. He asked God for signs, then routed Midian with 300 men. He refused to be king, but the gold ephod he made became a snare.

roles.name: Called
roles.line: By an angel, under an oak

lines: He made an ephod of them

tidbits.text: His name comes from a Hebrew word for **cutting down**. His first task was to cut down the Asherah pole beside his father's altar.

cite.text: Strong's Hebrew 1439, at Bible Hub; Judges 6:25

tidbits.text: He turned down a crown. Yet he named one of his sons **Abimelech**, which means “father is king”.

cite.text: Judges 8:31; Strong's Hebrew 40, at Bible Hub

tidbits.text: **The Gideons**, who put Bibles in hotel rooms, were founded by three travelling salesmen in 1899. Their emblem is a two-handled **pitcher and torch**, for his night attack.

facts.label: Home
facts.text: **Ophrah**, his hometown, in the land of the tribe of **Manasseh**. His father's oak stood there, and later the altar and the ephod Gideon made.

facts.label: Clan
facts.text: **Abiezer**, of the tribe of Manasseh. “My clan is the weakest in Manasseh,” he said.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: His father was **Joash** the Abiezrite. His brothers, “the sons of my mother”, were killed by the kings of Midian at Tabor. He had **many wives** and **seventy sons**: **Jether** was the eldest, **Jotham** the youngest. A concubine in Shechem bore him **Abimelech**.

facts.label: Work
facts.text: A **farmer**: the angel found him threshing wheat. Then a **judge** of Israel, one of the leaders God raised up to save it.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Jerubbaal**, “Let Baal contend with him”, after he tore down Baal's altar. **Jerubbesheth**, in 2 Samuel. **Gedeon**, in older Catholic books.

facts.label: His enemy
facts.text: **Midian**, with the **Amalekites** and other peoples of the east. For seven years they came up at harvest and stripped the land.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: “At a ripe old age”, says Judges. He was buried in the tomb of his father Joash, at **Ophrah**.

facts.label: In the New Testament
facts.text: Named first in the list of judges in **Hebrews 11**, among those “who through faith conquered kingdoms”.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: Kneeling by the **fleece**, often in armour, with an angel above, as in the panel here. In Russian icons he stands among the **prophets**, holding a scroll.

portrait.alt: A painting in a wooden frame: Gideon, grey-bearded, in armour and a red cloak, kneels on rocky ground holding a halberd and looks up at a white-robed angel flying in the sky. A fleece lies on the ground beside him. Tall rocks and thin pine trees stand behind. Latin words run along the top and the foot of the frame.
portrait.credit: The Fleece of Gideon, Nicolas Dipre, about 1500. Musée du Petit Palais, Avignon. Public domain.
portrait.creator: Nicolas Dipre
portrait.caption: Gideon kneels by the fleece as the angel appears. Nicolas Dipre of Avignon painted it about 1500. The Latin at the foot is Psalm 72:6, the verse of rain falling on a fleece. Public domain.

typeNote: The test names him for his fear, and for what he did with it. “My clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father’s house,” he said. He was afraid of his family and his town, but he still tore down Baal's altar. He did it at night.

west.text: With **Joshua**, in the **1916 Roman Martyrology**. He has no day in the calendar used at Mass today.

east.text: The **Coptic** Church, on 16 Kiahk in its own calendar: his departure.

feasts.note: Orthodox churches on the old calendar keep the Greek and OCA dates 13 days later. The Coptic 16 Kiahk falls on 26 December in the year before a leap year.

said.lede: His son, Samuel, Isaiah, the letter to the Hebrews and later writers, in their own words.

moments.title: The angel at the winepress
moments.text: For seven years Midian had raided Israel at every harvest, “like a great swarm of locusts”. Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress, to hide it from them. The angel of the LORD sat down under the oak and said, “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor.” Gideon answered, “If the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us?” The LORD said, “Go in the strength you have and save Israel from the hand of Midian. Am I not sending you?” Gideon said his clan was the weakest in Manasseh, and he the youngest in his family. “Surely I will be with you,” the LORD replied.

moments.title: Baal's altar, torn down by night
moments.text: That night the LORD told him to tear down his father's altar to Baal and cut down the Asherah pole beside it. Gideon took ten of his servants and did it. But he was too afraid of his father's household and the men of the town to do it by day, so he did it by night. In the morning the town found out who had done it. They told his father, “Bring out your son. He must die.” Joash stood by his son. “If Baal is a god, let him contend for himself with the one who has torn down his altar.” So Gideon was called Jerubbaal: “Let Baal contend with him.”

moments.title: The ram's horn
moments.text: Midian and its allies crossed the Jordan and camped in the Valley of Jezreel. Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon. He blew the ram's horn, and his own clan rallied behind him. He sent messengers through Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali, and they came up to meet him. Before he fought, he asked God for a sign with a fleece of wool. It is told with the miracles, below.

moments.title: From 32,000 to 300
moments.text: Gideon camped by the spring of Harod. The LORD said to him, “You have too many men for Me to deliver Midian into their hands, lest Israel glorify themselves over Me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’” Anyone afraid could go home. Twenty-two thousand left, and ten thousand stayed. “There are still too many men.” Gideon took them down to the water. Three hundred lapped it with their hands to their mouths. All the others knelt to drink. “With the three hundred men who lapped the water I will save you.”

moments.title: The barley loaf
moments.text: That night the LORD told him to attack. “But if you are afraid to do so, then go down to the camp with your servant Purah.” So he went. The enemy filled the valley like locusts, with camels “as countless as the sand on the seashore.” Gideon crept close and heard a man telling his friend a dream. A loaf of barley bread had come tumbling into the camp and knocked a tent flat. His friend said, “This is nothing less than the sword of Gideon son of Joash.” Gideon bowed in worship, and went back to wake his men.

moments.title: Jars, torches and horns
moments.text: He split the three hundred into three companies. Each man carried a ram's horn in one hand and a large jar in the other, with a torch inside it. “Watch me and do as I do,” Gideon said. Just after the changing of the guard, they blew their horns and smashed their jars. Holding up the torches, they shouted, “A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!” The whole Midianite army fled, crying out as they ran, and the LORD set them against one another with their swords.

moments.title: A soft answer
moments.text: Gideon called out the tribe of Ephraim to hold the fords of the Jordan. They caught Oreb and Zeeb, the two princes of Midian. Then they turned on Gideon. “Why did you fail to call us when you went to fight against Midian?” They argued with him hotly. Gideon made little of his own part. “Are not the gleanings of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer?” When he said this, their anger died down.

moments.title: Exhausted, yet still in pursuit
moments.text: Gideon crossed the Jordan with his three hundred, “exhausted yet still in pursuit.” He asked the town of Succoth for bread. Its leaders mocked him: had he caught the kings of Midian yet? Penuel gave the same answer. He caught the two kings, Zebah and Zalmunna, and on the way back he kept his threats. He punished the elders of Succoth with thorns and briers, pulled down the tower of Penuel and killed its men. The kings had killed his brothers at Tabor. “If you had let them live, I would not kill you.” He told his eldest son, Jether, to kill them. The boy was afraid and did not draw his sword, so Gideon killed them himself.

moments.title: A crown refused, an ephod made
moments.text: The Israelites asked him to rule over them, and his son and grandson after him. He turned them down. Then he made one request: a gold earring from each man's plunder. They spread out a garment and threw the earrings on it, 1,700 shekels of gold, besides the kings' ornaments and purple robes. From all this Gideon made an ephod and set it up in Ophrah. “But soon all Israel prostituted themselves by worshiping it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and his household.” Judges does not say what the ephod looked like. In Exodus an ephod is a garment of the high priest. *Britannica* calls Gideon's an idolatrous image.

miracles.lede: Gideon's first words to the angel were a question. Where had God's wonders gone?

pledge.q: And where are all His wonders of which our fathers told us, saying, ‘Has not the LORD brought us up out of Egypt?’

items.title: Fire from the rock
items.text: Gideon asked for a sign that it was really God speaking to him. He brought out a young goat, unleavened bread and broth. The angel told him to lay the meat and bread on a rock and pour out the broth. Then the angel touched them with the tip of his staff.
items.quote: And fire flared from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened bread.
items.witness: Then the angel vanished. Gideon built an altar on the spot and called it The LORD Is Peace.

items.title: Dew on the fleece
items.text: Gideon said to God, “If You are going to save Israel by my hand, as You have said,” then let there be dew on a fleece of wool, and all the ground dry. He laid the fleece on the threshing floor overnight.
items.quote: he squeezed the fleece and wrung out the dew—a bowlful of water

items.title: The fleece dry
items.text: Then he asked for one more test, begging God not to be angry. This time, let the fleece be dry and the ground wet.
items.quote: And that night God did so. Only the fleece was dry, and dew covered the ground.

extras.title: The fleece
extras.lede: The two nights of the fleece are the best-known part of his story. The early Church read them as a picture of things to come. Here are three readings, each in its own words.

items.title: Israel and the nations
items.text: Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons about 180, saw the wet fleece as Israel, which had the dew of the Spirit first. The second sign, dew on all the ground, showed the Spirit poured out on the whole world. Augustine read it as grace: in the old covenant it was “hidden in a cloud, as the rain in the fleece”, and now “the whole world, like that floor, is full of grace”.
items.quote: the dew, which is the Spirit of God, Who descended upon the Lord, should be diffused throughout all the earth

cite.text: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 17; Augustine, Sermon 81 on the New Testament

items.title: Not doubt, but care
items.text: Did asking twice show a weak faith? Ambrose of Milan put that question in 381, at the start of his book *On the Holy Spirit*. His answer was no. Gideon was “speaking in mysteries”, and “the words of God come down like the dew.”
items.quote: He was not then doubtful, but careful that we should not doubt.

cite.text: Ambrose, On the Holy Spirit, Book 1, introduction

items.title: Mary and the dew
items.text: In the Greek and Latin Bibles, Psalm 72 says the King “shall come down like rain upon a fleece”. Ambrose joined that verse to Gideon's fleece. Later hymns made the fleece a picture of Mary, who received the Word as the fleece received the dew. The *Akathist Hymn* greets her as the fleece Gideon saw beforehand. The OCA's life of Gideon quotes a hymn for her Entry into the Temple. It calls her the bright cloud through which the Lord came down, as dew falls on a fleece. Dipre's panel, above, has the psalm verse in Latin at its foot.

cite.text: Ambrose, Concerning Widows, chapter 3; Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lecture 12; the OCA, “The Righteous Gideon”; the Akathist Hymn, as quoted by John Sanidopoulos

feature.kicker: When they offered him a crown
feature.q: I will not rule over you, nor will my son. The LORD shall rule over you.
feature.ctx: After the victory, the Israelites said to him, “Rule over us—you and your son and grandson—for you have saved us from the hand of Midian.”

quotes.q: Oh no, Lord GOD! I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face!
quotes.who: When the angel vanished after the fire from the rock. The LORD answered, “Peace be with you. Do not be afraid, for you will not die.”

quotes.q: Get up, for the LORD has delivered the camp of Midian into your hand.
quotes.who: To his men, straight after he heard the Midianite's dream.

quotes.q: God has delivered Oreb and Zeeb, the two princes of Midian, into your hand. What was I able to do compared to you?
quotes.who: To the angry men of Ephraim.

myths.claim: Putting out a fleece is the Bible's way to find out God's will.
myths.truth: Gideon was not asking what God wanted. God had already told him, and Gideon says so twice: “as You have said”. He asked for the sign to be sure of it. The second time, he began, “Do not be angry with me”. Judges tells what he did. It never tells anyone to do the same. For how the early Church read the fleece, see The fleece, above.

myths.claim: God chose the 300 because they lapped like alert soldiers, with their eyes up.
myths.truth: Judges gives one reason for making the army small, and it is about God, not the men: so that Israel could not say its own hand had saved it. It never says why the lappers were the ones kept. Old readers took it both ways. Gregory of Nazianzus praised “the three hundred men with Gideon, who bravely lapped”. Josephus, writing about 93, says the opposite. God told Gideon that those who drank “tumultuously” did it “out of fear”, and those were the three hundred.

cite.text: Judges 7:2-7; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 42; Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book 5, chapter 6

circle.name: Joash
circle.text: His father. The altar to Baal was his. When the town wanted Gideon dead, Joash told them Baal could fight for himself.

circle.name: Purah
circle.text: His servant, who went down with him by night to listen at the edge of the Midianite camp.

circle.name: Jether
circle.text: His eldest son. Told to kill the captured kings, he did not draw his sword: “he was fearful because he was still a youth.”

circle.name: Abimelech
circle.text: His son by a concubine in Shechem. After Gideon died, he killed his seventy brothers and made himself king. At Thebez a woman dropped a millstone on his head, and his armour-bearer ran him through.

circle.name: Jotham
circle.text: His youngest son, the only one to escape Abimelech. From Mount Gerizim he told Shechem the fable of the trees that went looking for a king, and only the thornbush would take the job.

circle.name: Zebah and Zalmunna
circle.text: The two kings of Midian. They had killed his brothers at Tabor, men “each one resembling the son of a king.”

circle.name: Oreb and Zeeb
circle.text: The two princes of Midian, caught by the men of Ephraim at the rock of Oreb and the winepress of Zeeb. Psalm 83 still prays, “Make their nobles like Oreb and Zeeb”.

death.title: How he died, and after
death.big: He died “at a ripe old age” and was buried in his father's tomb at Ophrah.
paras: Midian “did not raise its head again”. The land had rest for forty years in his days, and he went home to Ophrah and settled down.
As soon as he was dead, Israel turned back to the Baals. They “did not show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) for all the good things he had done for Israel.”

His son Abimelech hired “worthless and reckless men”, went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his seventy brothers “on one stone”. Only Jotham, the youngest, hid and lived. The leaders of Shechem made Abimelech king.

He ruled for three years. Attacking a tower at Thebez, he came up to its entrance to burn it, and a woman dropped a millstone on his head. Judges closes the story: “In this way God repaid the wickedness that Abimelech had done to his father in murdering his seventy brothers.”

saint.big: He is honoured as a saint in the Orthodox and Catholic calendars, among the righteous of the Old Testament. Protestant churches keep no day for him, but Hebrews 11 names him among the faithful.

churches.note: Named in Hebrews 11 among the faithful

paras: Rome's book of martyrs, in its 1916 edition, keeps him on 1 September together with Joshua, “In Palestine”.
The Greek synaxarion keeps his day on 26 September. The OCA keeps it on 26 November, and its life of him quotes a hymn to Mary that speaks of the fleece.
The Coptic synaxarium remembers his departure on 16 Kiahk, as one of the judges of Israel.
